title: The FDA AdCom Rejects Brexpiprazole/Sertraline for PTSD this Week
subtitle: The FDA AdCom votes 10-1 against...
body_html:
It’s been a tough week for Lundbeck/Otsuka. Their combo pill—smooshing together Rexulti and Zoloft, if we are using brand names, was put through clinical trials for use in PTSD. This was submitted to the FDA. It went…poorly.

To recap the “small-molecule” oral medicines with evidence for PTSD…well, it’s really slim.

Only two drugs currently have an FDA label— Zoloft alone and Paxil, for PTSD. Other medicines have evidence, such as prazosin and Effexor, but the treatment landscape is limited.

This is one of the reasons people have been so excited about psychedelic medicines like MDMA, which also didn’t make it through its AdCom—short for advisory committee.

Prior Articles on the MDMA topic include:

Can MDMA-AT Be Saved, Part I

Can MDMA-AT Be Saved, Part II

Should MDMA-AT Be Saved, Part III

Saving MDMA from AT: Part IV

Bad Touch!: MDMA Part V

Saving MDMA Part IV

We have a Cochrane Review:

The findings of this review support the conclusion that SSRIs improve PTSD symptoms; they are first‐line agents for the pharmacotherapy of PTSD, based on moderate‐certainty evidence. The NaSSA mirtazapine and the TCA amitriptyline may also improve PTSD symptoms, but this is based on low‐certainty evidence.

The data set for that conclusion includes:

We include 66 RCTs in the review (range: 13 days to 28 weeks; 7442 participants; age range 18 to 85 years) and 54 in the meta‐analysis

Given that my readers are apt to be data nerds, I will get EVEN MORE detailed:

we found evidence of beneficial effect for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) compared with placebo (risk ratio (RR) 0.66,… which improved PTSD symptoms in 58% of SSRI participants compared with 35% of placebo participants, based on moderate‐certainty evidence.

And the authors highlight:

There remain important gaps in the evidence base, and a continued need for more effective agents in the management of PTSD.

And three reviewers of the Cochrane group made sure to add:

In addition, we found no evidence of benefit for the number of participants who improved following treatment with the antipsychotic group compared to placebo, based on very low‐certainty evidence.

This didn’t stop Lundbeck from mixing up a batch of brexpiprazole/sertraline—combining an antipsychotic and an SSRI, to see if they could tempt the fates by finally proving an antipsychotic did something useful! Except, the AdCom disagreed, 10-1 against.

If you like long-form video, here it is…

And if you don’t—I got you!

The FDA is split into different departments. Medications, like this submission, are reviewed by experts in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research.

The combo of these two drugs is a supplemental application to add an indication, on top of the already proposed treatment of agitation associated with alzheimer’s dementia. Brexpiprazole is a close cousin of aripiprazole (also known as Abilify, the subject of more chapters in my book “Inessential Pharmacology” (Amazon affiliate link) than any other drug).

The study for this combo drug was the largest-scale PTSD research program of all time. Over 1200 adults were in the three studies. There were 3 RCTs in total, and given there have only been two approved (drug) treatments in the past 25 years for PTSD, the time—as MAPS/Lykos was keen to remind us when they went through this process—is now. Or was supposed to be.

Thirteen million people in the US will have PTSD in any given year. 600/100,000 will have PTSD in their lifetime. It has a two times higher incidence rate in women than in men. That, in part, is likely to be due to the vastly higher rates of Child Sexual Abuse in girls, as covered earlier this week.

However, only 2 of the 3 studies in this research program were separated from the placebo. The Phase II trial was successful, and it led to one of the Phase III trials achieving its primary endpoint. The other Phase III trials didn’t separate. The FDA usually requires two replicated trials. As one AdCom member put it:

“The evidence from these two phase III trials is strong—it’s just in opposite directions!”

The open comments were, as usual, the spicy comments. Speaker #1, for example, notes:

“PTSD is a cage…it’s pop-up ads…for a horror movie based on actual events.”

I love members of the public. Speaker #1 has lived experience—can you tell? He was not mincing words. He was also in favor of this drug getting approved, because the need was dire.

Speaker #2 spoke on behalf of a rural mental health non-profit, in support of small-molecule treatments like this combination therapeutic:

“Military veterans are over-represented in rural communities…combat exposure might increase PTSD risk….access to care in rural areas is a real stumbling block…stigma…can be even more pronounced in rural communities.”

Moving on…Speaker #7 wasn’t into it:

“It’s statistical gymnastics…this application proposes starting two psychiatric medicines on day one…both drugs have severe withdrawal profiles…once again, the burden of risk will fall on the patients….the real harm unfolds in the real world. This is a market-extension strategy, not a medical breakthrough…please reject this application.”

Speaker #8 is a veteran. Otsuka covered his travel expenses, and he advocated approving the drug:

“When I started the military, they told us that each one of us has a bullet with our name on it…I started having panic attacks at the grocery store…even on my own couch. I’m here to remind you that a veteran dies by suicide every 11 minutes. 15-35% of veterans experience PTSD, and many of us develop PTSD from non-combat trauma like sexual assault…I realized that the bullet with my name on it might be the one in my own [gun’s] chamber.”

Sexual assault—it is poison for men too, even in the military. Speaker #8, a man, took a real risk speaking out like he did. Thank him for his service. His PTSD is just as disabling, even though it wasn’t from combat.

In the end, similar to the impassioned pleas from Otsuka/Lundbeck and its appropriately compensated commenters, the AdCom recommended 10-1 to decline this application.

To be clear, I applaud my colleagues at Otsuka and Lundbeck for taking on the challenge. It is crucial to have more PTSD treatment options. However, FDA approval shouldn’t be trivial, and prescribing clinicians need to be assured of the safety and efficacy of their tools. This is one that (probably) didn’t clear the bar. The advisory committee vote isn’t binding, but the overwhelming majority were clear in their decision—the data isn’t there yet.
